primer.amr_p_world.title: Two worlds of America
primer.amr_p_world.text: You were born in fifteenth-century America, a land Europe knows nothing about yet. Two great powers rise here, and neither has ever heard of the other. In the Valley of Mexico the Mexica of Tenochtitlan are on the rise, and dozens of cities send them tribute in cloth, cacao and feathers. In the Andes the Incas are building Tawantinsuyu, "the four parts together", a realm thousands of kilometres long. Neither has iron, horses or carts, yet their capitals will astonish the first Spaniards more than the cities of Spain.
primer.amr_p_world_tepanec.title: Under the Tepanecs
primer.amr_p_world_tepanec.text: The lake does not belong to the Mexica yet. The strongest man in the valley is old Tezozomoc, ruler of the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, and Tenochtitlan pays him tribute in fish, ducks and reed mats. The Mexica rulers Huitzilihuitl and Chimalpopoca marry into Tepanec families and fight their wars. In 1418 the Tepanecs killed Ixtlilxochitl, lord of Texcoco, and his young son Nezahualcoyotl fled into the hills. When Tezozomoc dies, around 1427, a war will break out that turns the valley upside down.
primer.amr_p_world_alliance.title: The Triple Alliance
primer.amr_p_world_alliance.text: In 1428 the Mexica under Itzcoatl, the Texcoco of Nezahualcoyotl and little Tlacopan jointly crushed Azcapotzalco and formed the Triple Alliance. Now tribute flows into the valley from the shores of both oceans: cacao, cotton, jade, quetzal feathers, maize and beans. The tlatoque of Tenochtitlan - Moctezuma the Elder, Axayacatl, Ahuitzotl, Moctezuma the Younger - push the borders outward one after another. Not everywhere, though: neighbouring Tlaxcala never submits, and the Tarascans in the west cannot be beaten.
primer.amr_p_world_cortes.title: Strangers from the sea
primer.amr_p_world_cortes.text: In 1519 bearded strangers landed on the eastern coast: the Spaniards of Hernán Cortés, about five hundred men with horses, cannon and steel swords. Thousands of Tlaxcalans and other enemies of the Mexica joined them. Moctezuma welcomed the guests into his capital, became their prisoner and died in 1520. Then came smallpox, a disease no one here had known, and it killed vast numbers, among them the new tlatoani Cuitlahuac. In August 1521, after a long siege, Tenochtitlan fell, and its last ruler, Cuauhtemoc, was taken captive.
primer.amr_p_world_newspain.title: New Spain
primer.amr_p_world_newspain.text: Tenochtitlan is gone. On its ruins the Spaniards are building Mexico City, capital of New Spain, and the stones of the temples go into churches and the conquerors' houses. People and land are handed out to Spaniards as encomiendas: the natives owe them tribute and labour. In 1524 twelve Franciscan friars arrived and began baptising thousands. The local nobility still run their neighbourhoods, but under watch; Cuauhtemoc was executed in 1525. In 1535 the first viceroy, Antonio de Mendoza, will arrive.
primer.amr_p_world_cusco_early.title: A small mountain kingdom
primer.amr_p_world_cusco_early.text: For now the Incas are just one of many highland peoples, and Cusco is a modest town in a valley 3,400 metres up. Viracocha Inca rules lands you could cross on foot in a few days. All around are neighbours the Incas marry one year and fight over fields and pastures the next. The most dangerous are the Chanka to the west, who, the story goes, are preparing to march on Cusco. No one yet suspects that this valley will soon be the heart of the largest empire in the Americas.
primer.amr_p_world_pachacuti.title: The world-turner
primer.amr_p_world_pachacuti.text: Legend says that when the Chanka reached Cusco, old Viracocha fled, while his son Cusi Yupanqui held the city and took the name Pachacuti, "he who turns the world over". This is usually dated to 1438, though the exact years are debated. Pachacuti rebuilt Cusco in stone and began the conquests, and his son Topa Inca campaigned from Lake Titicaca to the coastal kingdom of Chimor and the mountains of Quito. Conquered peoples keep their own lords, but their sacred objects are taken to Cusco and their people put to work for the empire.
primer.amr_p_world_huayna.title: Huayna Capac
primer.amr_p_world_huayna.text: Huayna Capac rules as Sapa Inca, "the only lord". The empire runs 4,000 kilometres along the Andes, and he spends years in the north, at Tomebamba and Quito, putting down the stubborn Cañari and Caranqui. Chasqui runners race along the roads, and the stone storehouses hold food for years. From the coast come rumours of strange bearded men in enormous boats. Around 1527 Huayna Capac died of an unknown illness, perhaps smallpox arriving ahead of the Spaniards themselves, and left no undisputed heir.
primer.amr_p_world_civilwar.title: War of the brothers
primer.amr_p_world_civilwar.text: Huayna Capac's sons are splitting the empire: Huascar rules in Cusco, while Atahualpa holds the north and their father's army near Quito. The brothers' war lays waste to the highlands, and in 1532 Atahualpa's generals Quizquiz and Chalcuchimac defeat and capture Huascar; his kin in Cusco are slaughtered. That same year at Cajamarca, fewer than two hundred Spaniards under Francisco Pizarro seized Atahualpa in the middle of the square, surrounded by thousands of his men. The empire was left without a head.
primer.amr_p_world_pizarro.title: Spaniards in the Andes
primer.amr_p_world_pizarro.text: Atahualpa paid his ransom, a room filled with gold and silver, yet in the summer of 1533 the Spaniards executed him. In November they entered Cusco and crowned young Manco, Huascar's brother, expecting an obedient puppet. The golden plates of the Temple of the Sun are being melted into bars. In the north the general Rumiñahui fought on, but in 1534 the Spaniards took Quito and founded their own town there. Many peoples tired of Inca rule are helping the newcomers, at least for now.
primer.amr_p_society.title: Nobles and commoners
primer.amr_p_society.text: In both worlds a ruler and his nobles stand at the top, and below them are the commoners who feed everyone. In Mexico the nobles are called pipiltin and the commoners macehualtin. In the Andes the summit belongs to the Incas by blood, with huge gold plugs in their ears, while the empire rests on the hatun runa, "the great people", the ordinary villagers. You can rise: a Mexica by taking captives in battle, an Andean craftsman by winning the Inca's favour. But most people born commoners live out their lives among their own.
primer.amr_p_society_mex.title: Pipiltin and macehualtin
primer.amr_p_society_mex.text: At the top sits the tlatoani, "he who speaks", with his chief counsellor, the cihuacoatl; behind them come the pipiltin, noble families who wear cotton and govern. Everything rests on the macehualtin: they live in calpolli wards, receive land from the ward, pay tribute and go to war. Below them are the mayeque, landless labourers on noble estates, and the tlacotin, the bonded. Merchants (pochteca) and craftsmen stand apart: rich, but careful to look modest so as not to anger the nobles. A warrior who takes four captives can climb very high.
primer.amr_p_society_and.title: Incas, curacas, villagers
primer.amr_p_society_and.text: Above all stands the Sapa Inca, son of the Sun. Below him are the Incas by blood, the "long-ears" with gold discs in their earlobes, and the Incas by privilege, neighbouring peoples allowed to wear Inca insignia. Conquered peoples are governed by curacas, local lords left in place. The empire rests on the hatun runa, the villagers, who are counted in tens, hundreds and thousands, each ten with its own headman. There are also the yana, lifelong servants, and the mitmaq, whole communities moved to distant provinces.
primer.amr_p_society_slave_mex.title: Tlacotli
primer.amr_p_society_slave_mex.text: You belong to the tlacotin, the bonded people. Most fall into bondage through poverty: selling themselves or their children in a famine year, gambling themselves away, working off a theft. Yet this is not Old World slavery. A tlacotli may have a family, belongings, even servants of his own, and by custom a tlacotli's children count as free, though poverty often keeps the whole family bound to the same household. Worst off are those sold on again and again. Buying your freedom, or receiving it from a master, is possible.
primer.amr_p_society_slave_and.title: Yana
primer.amr_p_society_slave_and.text: You come from the yana, lifelong servants. The Incas have no slave markets, but the yana have been cut off from their home ayllu: they owe none of the usual labour turns and instead serve a master - the Inca, a noble house, a temple or the mummy of a past ruler. They herd flocks, farm noble estates and run palace households. The status usually passes to the children. Still, a trusted yana can rise far: some became stewards and even curacas, and under the Spaniards many yana went over to serve new masters.
primer.amr_p_society_peasant_mex.title: A calpolli family
primer.amr_p_society_peasant_mex.text: You are one of the macehualtin, the common people. Your family belongs to a calpolli, a ward of kinsfolk with its own land, temple, school and elder. The ward gives each family a plot for as long as it works it; by custom a field left fallow for two years is taken back. In return come tribute, labour on public works and war. Many families by the lake farm chinampas, beds built up from lake mud right in the water, and harvest several crops a year.
primer.amr_p_society_peasant_and.title: Ayllu villagers
primer.amr_p_society_peasant_and.text: You are one of the hatun runa, the villagers. Land belongs to the ayllu, the kin group, and is shared out by the number of mouths: a plot called a tupu for a married couple and another piece for each child. First everyone works the fields of the Sun and of the Inca together, then their own. On top of that the men take turns at mit'a, labour for the state: building roads, hauling stone, serving in the army. There is hardly any tax in goods; the state takes labour and, in a bad year, feeds people from its storehouses.
primer.amr_p_society_noble_mex.title: Among the pipiltin
primer.amr_p_society_noble_mex.text: You were born among the pipiltin, the nobility. Nobles live in stone palaces with inner courtyards and gardens, and wear cotton, feathers and jade. Their sons attend the calmecac, a strict temple school that teaches writing, the calendar, the art of speech and the law. Judges, tribute collectors, envoys and generals are chosen from the pipiltin. But more is expected of them too: drunkenness that would get a commoner's head shaved in public could cost a noble his life.
primer.amr_p_society_noble_and.title: Incas by blood
primer.amr_p_society_noble_and.text: You were born into a royal ayllu, among the Incas by blood. Every dead ruler leaves behind a lineage, a panaca, whose members keep his mummy, his fields and his fame. Noble boys are taught language, religion, warfare and quipu reckoning in Cusco, and as youths they pass the warachikuy trials and have their ears pierced for their first gold plugs. The nobility own the finest cloth, ride in litters and command respect; governors, generals and priests are drawn from their ranks.
primer.amr_p_birth.title: Birth
primer.amr_p_birth.text: In both worlds midwives deliver babies, and a birth is the business of the gods. In Mexico the midwife greets the newborn with a long, solemn speech, and a priest checks which calendar sign the child was born under. In the Andes the baby is washed in cold water and will not get a name for a year or two. Many children die before their first birthday, so joy always comes mixed with worry and prayer. For the first days the mother barely gets up, and relatives bring her food and gifts.
primer.amr_p_birth_mex.title: The sign of your day
primer.amr_p_birth_mex.text: The midwife who caught you spoke to you at once: you had come into a world of toil and sorrow. A boy's umbilical cord is given to a warrior to bury on a battlefield; a girl's is buried by the hearth, where her place will be. A priest consults the book of days, where some signs promise luck and others misfortune. A few days later, on a favourable day, the baby is bathed and named, often after a day sign such as Ce Tochtli, "One Rabbit". A boy is given a tiny shield and arrows, a girl a spindle and a little broom.
primer.amr_p_birth_and.title: No name yet
primer.amr_p_birth_and.text: Andean women give birth kneeling, often with just one kinswoman beside them, and are back at work within days. The newborn is washed in a cold stream and laid in a quirau, a wooden cradle the mother carries on her back. You have no name yet. You will get one in a year or two at the rutuchikuy, "the first haircut": a senior relative will cut a lock of your hair and your nails, the family will bring gifts, and you will receive your childhood name.
primer.amr_p_childhood.title: Childhood
primer.amr_p_childhood.text: Childhood here is short. By five or six a child is already helping the family: fetching water, gathering firewood, scaring birds from the fields, minding animals. Girls learn to spin early and keep a spindle in hand until old age. Upbringing is strict, and laziness counts as a vice. Noble boys are sent to special schools to learn religion, reckoning, history and war. Toys are simple: clay whistles, little animal figures, small bows and spindles.
primer.amr_p_childhood_mex.title: Tortillas by age
primer.amr_p_childhood_mex.text: Children are raised strictly. The Codex Mendoza even shows how many tortillas a child gets: half at three, a whole one at four or five, one and a half later. Boys carry water and wood; girls start spinning at four. Disobedient children are pricked with agave spines, and the most stubborn are held over the smoke of burning chillies. On the other hand every Mexica boy goes to school, rare for the age: commoners to the telpochcalli, "house of youth", nobles to the temple calmecac.
primer.amr_p_childhood_and.title: A little worker
primer.amr_p_childhood_and.text: From five or six a child is a worker: scaring birds off the maize, gathering brushwood, herding llamas and alpacas on cold slopes. Girls pick up the spindle early and spin even while walking. Teaching is by doing, not by talking, and the lazy are punished. Noble boys go to Cusco, to the yachaywasi, "house of knowledge", where amauta sages teach them Quechua, religion, history and quipu reckoning. At fourteen or fifteen a boy goes through a rite and receives a man's loincloth.
primer.amr_p_home.title: Home
primer.amr_p_home.text: An ordinary home has one or two rooms with a hearth in the middle and no tables or chairs: people sit and sleep on mats or hides. Belongings are kept in baskets and clay jars. Relatives live around the same courtyard, so life is spent in full view of the family. Nobles live in stone palaces with gardens, and in the Andes behind walls of perfectly fitted stone. Hearth smoke seeps out through the thatch, so every house smells of smoke and roasted maize.
primer.amr_p_home_mex.title: A three-stone hearth
primer.amr_p_home_mex.text: An ordinary house has one or two rooms of adobe or mud-plastered wattle on a stone base, roofed with straw or reeds. There is almost no furniture: people sit and sleep on petlatl mats and keep their things in woven chests. The heart of the house is the three-stone hearth, the clay griddle (comalli) and the grinding stone (metlatl), where the women grind maize every morning. In the yard there are turkeys, little dogs and a small steam bath, the temazcalli.
primer.amr_p_home_and.title: Kancha and guinea pigs
primer.amr_p_home_and.text: A house is a single room with stone or adobe walls and a roof of ichu mountain grass; there are hardly any windows, to keep the warmth in, because the mountain nights bring frost. Several houses around a shared yard make up a kancha, home to an extended family. People sleep on the floor on hides and blankets. Guinea pigs, cuy, scurry around the corners; they live right in the house and are eaten on feast days. Maize dries under the roof, and wall niches hold jars and small guardian figurines.
primer.amr_p_food.title: Food
primer.amr_p_food.text: People here eat things the Old World has never seen: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, squash, chilli peppers, cacao. In Mexico the staple is the maize tortilla; in the Andes, hundreds of kinds of potato. Meat is rare: turkey, dog, guinea pig or dried llama. Strong drink - Mexican pulque from agave sap and Andean maize chicha - flows most freely at festivals. People usually eat twice a day, sitting on the floor around shared bowls.
primer.amr_p_food_mex.title: Maize, chilli, chocolate
primer.amr_p_food_mex.text: Everything starts with maize: tortillas, tamales steamed in husks, and thick atolli gruel. With it come beans, squash, tomatoes and chilli, without which food tastes bland. Protein comes from turkey, a special breed of dog, fish, frogs and even a blue-green algae skimmed from the lake and dried into cakes. Cacao chocolate is a drink for nobles and warriors; ordinary people cannot afford it. Pulque is drunk at festivals, and drunkenness among the young is severely punished.
primer.amr_p_food_and.title: Potatoes and chicha
primer.amr_p_food_and.text: In the highlands the staple is the potato, grown here in hundreds of varieties. It is left out in the night frost and trampled underfoot to make chuño, freeze-dried potato that keeps for years. People grow quinoa, oca and beans, and maize in the warmer valleys. From maize the women brew chicha, a cloudy, sour beer no festival or shared workday can do without. Meat, dried llama (charqui) or guinea pig, is not an everyday thing. Everything is seasoned with uchu chilli and salt.
primer.amr_p_clothes.title: Clothing
primer.amr_p_clothes.text: Cloth is worth more than almost anything here: it is given as a gift, paid as tribute and hoarded as wealth. Men wear a loincloth with a cloak or tunic; women wear a wrapped skirt or a long dress. Clothing shows at once who you are: coarse agave fibre or llama wool for commoners, fine cotton, feathers and vicuña wool for the nobility. Only those entitled to them wear gold, jade and feathers.
primer.amr_p_clothes_mex.title: A cloak you have earned
primer.amr_p_clothes_mex.text: Men wear a maxtlatl loincloth and a tilmatli cloak knotted at the shoulder; women wear a wrapped skirt and a huipilli blouse. Clothes say who you are: commoners get a rough agave-fibre cloak that may not fall below the knee, while cotton and bright patterns belong to nobles and renowned warriors. The laws of Moctezuma the Elder set out strictly who may wear what. Nobles adorn themselves with quetzal feathers, jade, ear spools and plugs set in the lower lip. A warrior who has taken captives earns a cloak with a special design, visible from afar.
primer.amr_p_clothes_and.title: Unku and tupu
primer.amr_p_clothes_and.text: Men wear the unku, a sleeveless knee-length tunic, and a yacolla cloak; women wear the anaku, a long wrapped dress fastened at the chest with a tupu pin, and a lliclla shawl. Every people in the empire must wear its own headdress, so you can tell from afar where someone comes from. Everyday cloth is coarse llama wool, while fine cumbi woven from vicuña wool is made for the Inca and the nobility and prized above gold. Inca nobles wear huge gold discs in their earlobes.
primer.amr_p_faith.title: Gods and spirits
primer.amr_p_faith.text: In Mexico and in the Andes alike, gods and spirits are everywhere: in mountains, springs, maize fields, the sun and the rain. People offer them flowers, food, cloth and blood, because the world runs on exchange: people feed the gods, and the gods feed people. The darkest page of this faith is human sacrifice, frequent among the Mexica, rare and exceptional among the Incas. After the Spaniards arrive, churches rise where temples stood, and people are baptised by the thousand.
primer.amr_p_faith_aztec.title: The Fifth Sun
primer.amr_p_faith_aztec.text: The Mexica believe they live in the age of the Fifth Sun, and that the sun must be fed or the world will end. The chief gods are Huitzilopochtli, god of sun and war; Tlaloc, who brings rain; Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent; and Tezcatlipoca, "Smoking Mirror". Everyone offers the gods their own blood, piercing their earlobes with agave spines. Captured warriors are sacrificed atop the pyramids, a grim duty the Mexica hold sacred. Once every 52 years the whole people puts out every fire and waits to see whether the New Fire will be kindled.
primer.amr_p_faith_andean.title: Sun and huaca
primer.amr_p_faith_andean.text: The Incas worship Inti, the Sun and ancestor of their kings, the creator Viracocha, the thunder god Illapa and Pachamama, Mother Earth. But closest to ordinary people are the huacas, sacred places and objects: a rock, a spring, a mountain, an ancestor's mummy. They receive coca, chicha, guinea pigs and llamas, and before drinking people flick a few drops on the ground for Pachamama. Dead rulers' mummies "live" in their palaces, are fed and carried out for festivals. In the rarest, gravest moments people were sacrificed, in the rite called capacocha.
primer.amr_p_faith_catholic.title: The new faith
primer.amr_p_faith_catholic.text: Your family has taken up the newcomers' religion. Franciscan friars, and Dominicans in the Andes, baptise people in crowds, give them names like Juan, María and Francisco, and teach prayers in the local language. The old temples are torn down and the statues of the gods smashed, while noble children are sent to mission schools; the first was opened in Texcoco in 1523 by the Flemish friar Pedro de Gante. Some converted sincerely, others out of fear or for advantage, and some still pray to the old gods in secret.
primer.amr_p_work.title: Work and tribute
primer.amr_p_work.text: Almost everyone here farms: maize, beans, potatoes, squash. The great powers live on the tribute and labour of the conquered. In Mexico tribute comes as cloth, cacao and feathers; in the Andes it is paid in work, in fields, on building sites and in the army. There is no money in our sense anywhere. Mexico has vast bustling markets, while the Inca heartland has almost none, because the state distributes everything. Craftsmen - weavers, potters, goldsmiths, stone carvers - work above all for nobles and temples.
primer.amr_p_work_mex.title: Cacao instead of coins
primer.amr_p_work_mex.text: There are no coins, but there is small change: little purchases are paid in cacao beans, big ones in cotton cloaks called quachtli, each worth somewhere between 65 and 300 beans depending on the source. The great market of Tlatelolco, the Spaniards said, drew tens of thousands of people: maize, chillies, cloth, obsidian, feathers, slaves and gold dust in goose quills. Farmers work their fields or chinampas, and craftsmen live in wards by trade. Canoes laden with tribute from conquered provinces glide into the capital all day long.
primer.amr_p_work_and.title: Ayni and mit'a
primer.amr_p_work_and.text: The Incas have no money, and the heart of the empire has almost no markets: everything runs on labour. Villagers help one another by the custom of ayni - I help you today, you help me tomorrow - and give the state mit'a, work by rotation, during which the workers are fed and plied with chicha. Harvests from the Inca's fields go into thousands of stone storehouses, qollqa, along the roads. Camayoc craftsmen weave, make pottery and work metal, fed by the state. Only in the north, around Quito, do mindalá merchants make the rounds of markets.
primer.amr_p_place.title: Your land
primer.amr_p_place.text: You live in one of the two hearts of the Americas. One is the Valley of Mexico: a highland lake ringed by dozens of cities, with Tenochtitlan on its island. The other is the Andes: mountains higher than any in Europe, terraced fields on the slopes and stone-built Cusco, "the navel of the world". Thousands of kilometres of forest and sea lie between them, and they will never learn of each other before the Spaniards come.
primer.amr_p_place_tenochtitlan.title: A city on the lake
primer.amr_p_place_tenochtitlan.text: Tradition says Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325 where the Mexica saw an eagle perched on a cactus. It is an island in the middle of the lake, tied to the shore by three causeways, with canals instead of streets and thousands of canoes gliding along them. Fresh water arrives by aqueduct from Chapultepec. Above the rooftops rises the Great Temple, the twin pyramid of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. Estimates put the population at one to two hundred thousand, more than any city in Spain at the time.
primer.amr_p_place_texcoco.title: The poet's city
primer.amr_p_place_texcoco.text: Texcoco, capital of the Acolhua on the eastern shore of the lake, is the second city of the Triple Alliance. It owes its fame to Nezahualcoyotl, who ruled from 1431 to 1472: poet, lawgiver and builder. To his design a dike some sixteen kilometres long was built to hold the lake's salt water back from the fresh water around Tenochtitlan, and on the hill of Texcotzinco he laid out gardens with baths cut into the rock. The most elegant Nahuatl is spoken here. The poet's son Nezahualpilli rules until 1515.
primer.amr_p_place_cusco.title: The navel of the world
primer.amr_p_place_cusco.text: Cusco, "the navel of the world", is a capital about 3,400 metres up. Legend says Pachacuti rebuilt it in the shape of a puma, with the fortress of Sacsayhuaman, built of stones weighing many tonnes, as its head. At the centre lies the Huacaypata square, where roads set out for the four quarters of the empire. The Temple of the Sun, Coricancha, is sheathed in gold plates. Commoners may not live in the centre: it belongs to noble palaces and the mummies of past rulers, each with its own servants and fields.
primer.amr_p_place_quito.title: Eternal spring
primer.amr_p_place_quito.text: Quito sits on a green mountain shelf about 2,800 metres up, almost on the equator, beneath the Pichincha volcano. There is no winter or summer here, just endless spring, rain and mist. The Incas arrived in the second half of the fifteenth century and took a long time to subdue the region: the Caranqui and Cañari resisted for years, and everyone here knows the story of the massacre at Yahuarcocha, "the lake of blood". Huayna Capac made Quito his northern base and settled loyal communities from the south around it.
primer.amr_p_law.title: Law and justice
primer.amr_p_law.text: The laws here are harsh, but order is firmly kept. Rulers, judges and community elders hear cases; theft and fraud are punished in public, grave crimes with death. Drunkenness, idleness and lying count as dangerous vices. There are no written law codes: in Mexico cases are painted into books, while in the Andes they are remembered and tallied on knotted cords. It is not only the culprit who answers: the family and the ward or village are held to account too. A noble is often punished more harshly than a commoner for the same crime.
primer.amr_p_law_mex.title: Court in the palace
primer.amr_p_law_mex.text: Mexica law is harsh. Courts sit in the palace from dawn to dusk, cases are recorded in pictures, and a judge who took a bribe could be put to death. A thief who cannot repay usually becomes the bondsman of the person he robbed. A drunken commoner has his head shaved in public the first time and may be executed the second; only the elderly may drink freely. Texcoco is famous for the laws of Nezahualcoyotl, who, they say, did not spare even his own son.
primer.amr_p_law_and.title: He who sees all
primer.amr_p_law_and.text: Order is kept by curacas and the headmen of each ten, and from time to time inspectors arrive from Cusco - "he who sees all". Idleness, lying and stealing from the common stores are punished in public; according to Spanish chroniclers, a minor offence earned a stone dropped on the back, a grave one death. Superiors answer too: if a man steals, his headman shares the blame. You may not wander the roads without business and permission; guards stand at the bridges.
primer.amr_p_health.title: Sickness and healing
primer.amr_p_health.text: Illness is taken for a punishment from the gods or the work of sorcery, so healers treat it with herbs and rituals alike. They know hundreds of medicinal plants, set bones and treat wounds. Before the Europeans arrive, nobody here knows smallpox, measles or influenza, and when those diseases come they kill more people than any war. The dead are honoured: in Mexico usually cremated, in the Andes dried, kept and brought food.
primer.amr_p_health_mex.title: Ticitl and temazcal
primer.amr_p_health_mex.text: Illness is sent by gods, sorcerers and evil omens, so the ticitl, the healer, treats it with herbs and prayers alike. The Mexica know hundreds of medicinal plants; they set bones, let blood and treat colds and exhaustion in the temazcal steam bath. The dead are usually cremated, and the soul spends four years travelling to Mictlan, the underworld, with a dog to help it along the way. Fallen warriors and women who die in childbirth go to the sun. From 1520 smallpox swept the valley and emptied whole neighbourhoods.
primer.amr_p_health_and.title: Coca and confession
primer.amr_p_health_and.text: Healers use herbs, coca and prayer, and diviners read a guinea pig's entrails to learn where an illness came from. Sickness is seen as punishment for sin: the patient confesses to a special priest and washes in a river. Andean surgeons can do something that still amazes scholars: they open the skull to treat head wounds, and many patients survive. The dead are not burned but dried and kept in caves and tombs, where they are brought food. Around 1527 an epidemic swept the Andes and killed Huayna Capac himself.
primer.amr_p_women.title: Women's lives
primer.amr_p_women.text: A woman here keeps the hearth and weaves: girls learn to spin and weave at four or five, and the cloth from her hands is real family wealth. Girls marry young, at fifteen to eighteen, by family arrangement. Women own property, trade, heal, deliver babies and serve the gods. Childbirth is considered dangerous, almost a battle, and a woman who dies giving birth is honoured. Women grind grain, cook, haul water and raise the children, and often work the fields beside their husbands. A widow usually stays with her husband's kin or soon remarries.
primer.amr_p_women_mex.title: The battle of birth
primer.amr_p_women_mex.text: From childhood a girl learns to spin, weave, cook and grind maize. Girls marry at fifteen to seventeen, through elderly women matchmakers, and at the wedding the hem of the groom's cloak is tied to the bride's blouse. A woman may own property, trade in the market, go to court, and work as a midwife, healer or priestess. The Mexica see childbirth as a battle: a woman who dies in labour is honoured like a fallen warrior and becomes a spirit, a cihuateotl. Mothers instruct their daughters: carry yourself modestly, speak softly, never sit idle.
primer.amr_p_women_and.title: Two halves
primer.amr_p_women_and.text: For the Incas, man and woman are two halves of a whole: he ploughs, she plants; he fights, she weaves for the army. Women spin constantly, walking, visiting, sitting by the fire. The most skilled girls are taken into the acllawasi, "house of the chosen women", where they weave fine cloth and brew chicha for the temples; some are given as wives to nobles. Adults are not expected to live unpaired. According to the chroniclers, from Topa Inca onward the Inca took his own sister as his principal wife.
primer.amr_p_leisure.title: Festivals and games
primer.amr_p_leisure.text: Festivals here are worship and merrymaking at once: processions, dances, flutes and drums, feasting and drink. The calendar is crowded with feasts tied to the sun, the rain, sowing and harvest. Adults gamble keenly with dice and marked beans, staking cloth and jewellery. Even shared field work goes with songs, food and drink. Poets and singers perform at noble courts, and dancers in masks and feathers fill the squares. Children play ball, race each other and imitate grown-up warriors.
primer.amr_p_leisure_mex.title: Patolli and the ballgame
primer.amr_p_leisure_mex.text: The Mexica year has eighteen "months" of twenty days, and almost every one brings a festival with dances, flutes, drums, processions and feasting. The last five days of the year, the nemontemi, are unlucky, so it is best to start nothing then. Adults gamble passionately at patolli, throwing marked beans and moving pebbles around a cross-shaped board, staking cloaks and even their freedom. The nobles watch the ballgame, where a heavy rubber ball is struck with the hips and aimed through a stone ring.
primer.amr_p_leisure_and.title: Festivals of the Sun
primer.amr_p_leisure_and.text: The great festivals follow the sun: Inti Raymi in June, in the shortest days of the year, and Capac Raymi in December, when noble youths pass their trials. The mummies of past rulers are carried out into the square of Cusco, and the capital drinks, sings and dances for days on end. People play quena flutes, panpipes and drums, and pass the time with dice and marked beans. But the best fun ordinary people know is shared work: the ploughing of the Inca's field is greeted with songs and chicha.
primer.amr_p_knowledge.title: Knowledge and reckoning
primer.amr_p_knowledge.text: There is no alphabet here, but knowledge is kept in its own ways. In Mexico people write in pictures in folding books of bark paper and hide; in the Andes they keep accounts on quipus, knotted cords. Calendars are precise and intricate, and priests watch the sun and stars. History, laws and prayers are learned by heart, and schools for noble youths train priests, judges and generals. Ordinary people cannot read the pictures or the cords - that is work for scribes and keepers - but everyone knows the songs and stories of the ancestors.
primer.amr_p_knowledge_mex.title: Folding books
primer.amr_p_knowledge_mex.text: The Mexica write in pictures: scribes called tlacuilo paint signs into long screenfold books of amatl bark paper or deerskin. They record tribute, genealogies, laws, field boundaries and the calendar. There are two calendars, a sacred one of 260 days and a solar one of 365, and together they come round again every 52 years. In the calmecac young men learn "the words of the ancients" and songs by heart. Texcoco is famous for its archives and poets: "Must I go like the flowers that have faded?" sang Nezahualcoyotl.
primer.amr_p_knowledge_and.title: Quipu knots
primer.amr_p_knowledge_and.text: The Incas have no writing, but they have the quipu, bundles of coloured cords tied with knots. The knots stand for units, tens and hundreds; the colour shows what is being counted: people, llamas, sacks of maize. Quipucamayoc, the keepers, know what every cord means and can report on a whole province from a quipu; whether quipus also stored stories is still debated by scholars. Poets and amauta sages keep the empire's history in memory, and the sun is tracked by stone pillars on the hills around Cusco.
primer.amr_p_war.title: War
primer.amr_p_war.text: Both empires were built by war. There is no iron and there are no horses: men fight with clubs, spears, slings, bows and spear-throwers, and wear quilted cotton instead of armour. The armies are huge, fed by tribute and storehouses. The conquered pay and serve, but many hate their overlords, and when the Spaniards come that will prove fatal. Every boy knows that one day he too will be called to campaign. A warrior who returns victorious earns honour and gifts, and those killed in battle are especially revered.
primer.amr_p_war_mex.title: Take a captive
primer.amr_p_war_mex.text: For a Mexica man, war is the main road to glory. Warriors fight with wooden macuahuitl swords edged with obsidian, with spear-throwers and bows, and wear a thick quilted cotton jacket instead of armour. The point is not to kill but to take a captive: each new prisoner earns a warrior cloaks and privileges, and the best become eagle and jaguar warriors. Against Tlaxcala they wage "flower wars", battles fought by agreement. Around 1479, though, the Tarascans crushed a Mexica army in the west.
primer.amr_p_war_and.title: An army on the roads
primer.amr_p_war_and.text: The Inca army is made of villagers doing their mit'a: they are raised by the tens of thousands, fed from roadside storehouses and marched along a royal road thousands of kilometres long. They fight with slings, clubs with star-shaped stone heads, spears and bolas. The Incas first offer surrender and promise gifts; those who submit keep their lord, while those who resist may be resettled, community and all. The main wars are now fought on the frontiers: in the north near Quito, and in the south by the Maule River.
